> Everything on https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/ that explains Keel, as Markdown: the docs, the roadmap and the blog. Index: https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/llms.txt

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/

# Keel documentation

Keel owns the part of your app that is not pixels: domain logic, reactive state, the data layer, persistence and the dev loop. These pages take you from an empty directory to a running app, then explain how the pieces work.

## Where to start

- **New here?** [Getting started](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/getting-started.html) installs the toolchain and CLI, scaffolds a project, runs the live dev loop and puts an app on each platform.
- **Writing a core?** [Core concepts](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/concepts.html) covers stores, signals, computeds and keyed lists. [Queries & mutations](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/queries.html) covers the data layer, and [Ports & adapters](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/ports.html) covers everything that touches the outside world.
- **Looking something up?** [The CLI](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/cli.html) lists every command and flag. [Architecture](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/architecture.html) explains the schema, the generators, the wire and the twelve rules. The API overviews show what a record, error, store or port looks like in [Swift](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/api-swift.html), [Kotlin](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/api-kotlin.html) and [TypeScript](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/api-typescript.html).

## The idea in four sentences

You write your domain in Rust and mark it with a handful of attributes. Keel generates idiomatic Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript from the schema those attributes produce, so the UI stays SwiftUI, Compose and React. Each platform keeps a local mirror of your state, so reads never cross the language boundary. A write crosses once per transaction, and the core answers with one compact binary change-set that patches every mirror.

**Where these pages come from.** Everything here is digested from the repository: the README, the specification in `docs/SPEC.md`, the onboarding guide, the benchmark results and the playground app. When a page and the spec disagree, the spec wins; the [repository](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel) is the record.

## A note on numbers

Performance figures on this site are host-measured (an Apple M5 Pro, release builds) and guarded by budgets in CI. They are not device numbers. The design's per-device targets (an iPhone, a mid-range Android phone, Chromium) are tracked in [bench/RESULTS.md](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md), and nothing on this site claims them as measured.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/getting-started.html

# Getting started

Install the toolchain, install the CLI, scaffold a project, and run it. A core you can test takes about ten minutes; the full five-language matrix takes about thirty including downloads.

Everything here was exercised end to end on an Apple-Silicon Mac, which is the reference environment. Linux paths differ only where noted in the repository's onboarding guide; Windows is untested.

## What you need

Install only what your target platforms need. `keel doctor` checks all of it and prints the fix for each gap.

| You want | You need |
| --- | --- |
| Any core (everything in `crates/`) | Rust stable, plus the cross targets Keel ships to |
| Web | Node 22+, and `binaryen` (for `wasm-opt`) |
| Android | JDK 17, Kotlin, Gradle, the Android SDK and NDK r27, `cargo-ndk` |
| iOS (macOS only) | Full Xcode from the App Store, plus an iOS simulator runtime |

## 1. Install the toolchain

Rust comes first, with the targets Keel builds for.

bash

```bash
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown \
  aarch64-apple-ios aarch64-apple-ios-sim \
  aarch64-linux-android x86_64-linux-android
```

Then the platform pieces you need.

bash

```bash
# Web and the TypeScript runtime
brew install node binaryen

# Android: JDK, Kotlin, Gradle, then the SDK and NDK
brew install openjdk@17 kotlin gradle
brew install --cask android-commandlinetools
cargo install cargo-ndk
```

For iOS, install Xcode from the App Store (the Command Line Tools alone have no XCTest and no simulators), then:

bash

```bash
sudo xcode-select -s /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer
sudo xcodebuild -license accept
xcodebuild -downloadPlatform iOS        # simulator runtime, one time, large
```

The Android SDK needs a few packages (platform 35, build-tools 35, NDK 27.2, the emulator and a system image). The [onboarding guide](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/docs/ONBOARDING.md) has the exact `sdkmanager` line and an `avdmanager` line that creates the `keel` emulator used throughout the project.

## 2. Install the CLI

Pick one channel. Homebrew, the curl installer and npm put a prebuilt `keel` binary on your machine; cargo builds it from source with Rust 1.85 or newer.

| Channel | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Homebrew | `brew install shreypdev/keel/keel` |
| npm | `npm install -g @keel/cli` |
| curl | `curl -fsSL https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/install.sh \| sh` |
| cargo | `cargo install --git https://github.com/shreypdev/keel keel-cli` |

The curl installer detects your OS and architecture, verifies the download against the release checksums, installs to `~/.keel/bin` and prints the line to add to your `PATH`. It never uses `sudo`.

bash

```bash
keel --version
keel doctor      # prints what is missing, with the fix
```

`keel doctor` exits with status 1 when something the project needs is missing, so it works in CI too. Inside a project it only checks the platforms named in `keel.toml`.

### From a checkout (contributors)

bash

```bash
git clone https://github.com/shreypdev/keel.git && cd keel
cargo install --path crates/keel-cli    # the `keel` command
source scripts/env.sh                   # PATH, JDK and Kotlin jars, Xcode fallback, per shell
```

## 3. Create a project

bash

```bash
keel init myapp                        # core + SwiftUI + Compose + React shells
keel init myapp --platforms ios,web    # only some of them
keel init myapp --id dev.acme.myapp    # application id / bundle identifier
cd myapp
```

Nothing is downloaded: the templates are part of the `keel` binary. The project you get is a directory with a `keel.toml` and:

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `core/` | The Rust core: a working to-do store with `#[keel::store]` and `#[keel::api]` |
| `generated/` | Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript bindings for that core, already generated |
| `ios/` `android/` `web/` | One minimal, real app per platform, using the generated bindings |

Pass `--keel-path ~/src/keel` (or set `KEEL_PATH`) to use a local checkout's crates and runtimes instead of released versions.

## 4. Start the live loop

bash

```bash
keel dev                          # serves the core on ws://127.0.0.1:7443
keel dev --addr 0.0.0.0:7443      # reachable from a phone on your network
```

`keel dev` runs your core on this machine and serves it over a WebSocket. A simulator, a phone or a browser tab connects with the `remote` transport of its runtime and uses this core instead of a built-in one. Edit Rust, save, and the core is rebuilt and restarted; reload the app to reconnect. Development log records (a line per transaction commit, port call and panic) print in the terminal.

**No authentication.** The server has none. Keep the default loopback address unless a device has to reach it, and never expose it beyond a network you trust.

## 5. Run each platform

Each shell is a plain native project wired to your core, and its own README says how to run it. The short version:

### Web

bash

```bash
cd web && npm install && npm run dev
```

The page loads the core as a wasm module. To use the core that `keel dev` serves instead, load it in `remote` mode:

ts

```ts
await KeelCore.load({ mode: "remote", url: "ws://127.0.0.1:7443", expectedSchemaHash: KeelIds.schemaHash });
```

### iOS

Open `ios/` in Xcode and run on a simulator. In debug builds the generated app reads `KEEL_DEV_URL` (for example `ws://<your Mac>:7443`) and attaches to `keel dev` when it is set.

Debug builds of the core need the library linked with `-force_load`, or the linker drops the core's registrations and the schema looks empty; the generated Xcode project already does this. Release builds need no flag.

### Android

Build the core with `keel build --platform android --release`, then build and install from `android/` with Gradle. Use `--release` for anything you run: a debug core is tens of megabytes per ABI. The Kotlin runtime has no remote transport on Android yet, so use the JVM or the web for the `keel dev` loop.

## 6. Build what you ship

bash

```bash
keel build --release        # every platform in keel.toml
keel build --platform ios,android,web --release
```

| Platform | Artifact, below `build/` |
| --- | --- |
| iOS | `ios/KeelCore.xcframework` (device and simulator slices) |
| Android | `android/jniLibs/<abi>/libkeel_core.so`, arm64-v8a and x86_64, 16 KB page aligned |
| Web | `web/keel_core.wasm`, release profile then `wasm-opt -Oz` |
| Host | `host/libkeel_core.{dylib,so}`, for JVM tests and `keel bindgen` |

Sizes are printed at the end next to the design's budgets. On the reference build the hello-world web core is 85 KB gzipped and an Android `.so` is 831 KB per ABI.

## Prefer to explore first?

Try it in your browser first: the [live playground](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/playground/) is the real Rust core running as WebAssembly. The [playground source](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/tree/main/examples/playground) is the same thing, fully built: a to-do list, a counter, a 10,000-row keyed list and remote queries with an offline switch, on Chrome, an iPhone simulator and an Android emulator. It uses only public APIs, and proof screenshots are committed in its `.proof/` folder.

bash

```bash
keel build -C examples/playground --platform web
cd examples/playground/web && npm install && npm run dev
```

## If you are contributing

Every suite runs locally and nothing needs the network after install. The table is the same one the CI matrix follows.

| Suite | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Rust workspace | `cargo test --workspace` |
| Lints | `cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` |
| TypeScript runtime | `cd runtimes/ts/@keel/runtime && npm ci && npm test` |
| Kotlin runtime | `runtimes/kotlin/keel-runtime/scripts/test-local.sh` |
| Swift runtime | `cd runtimes/swift/KeelRuntime && swift test` |
| wasm ABI | `bash crates/keel-ffi/tests/wasm/run.sh` |
| Contract scenarios, three platforms | `bash contract-tests/run-all.sh` |
| Benchmark budget gate | `cargo test -p keel-bench --test budgets --release` |

Read `CLAUDE.md` (the constitution) and `docs/SPEC.md` before you write code; the [architecture page](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/architecture.html#constitution) digests the rules. Changes land one piece per worktree, with an adversarial review before merge; `docs/AGENT_WORKFLOW.md` describes the loop for humans and agents alike.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/concepts.html

# Core concepts

State in Keel lives in the Rust core as signals inside stores. Platforms hold a local mirror, reads never cross the boundary, and a write crosses once per transaction.

## The building blocks

Everything a platform can see is one of eight kinds of thing, each declared with an attribute. They cross the boundary in one of two ways: by value (copied) or by handle (a reference to something that stays in the core).

| Concept | Declared with | Crosses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Record | `#[keel::api]` on a `struct` | by value |
| Enum | `#[keel::api]` on an `enum`, unit or data variants | by value |
| Error | `#[keel::error]` on an `enum`; adds `Display` and `std::error::Error` | by value |
| Object | `#[keel::api]` on an `impl` block; methods are sync or async | by handle |
| Store | an object whose struct has `#[keel::store]`; its signals are mirrored | by handle |
| Port | `#[keel::port]` on a trait; implemented by the platform or by a Rust fake | the core calls out to it |
| Query, mutation | `#[keel::query]`, `#[keel::mutation]` on an `async fn` | managed by the query client |
| Function | `#[keel::api]` on a free `fn` | like a method with no receiver |

The rest of this page is about stores, because that is where reactive state lives.

## Stores

A store is a struct of signals with an `impl` block that says what the platforms can call. The to-do list from the playground is a complete example:

core/src/todos.rs

```rust
#[keel::store(restore = "Self::assemble")]
pub struct Todos {
    next: AtomicU64,                       // private state: not a signal
    #[keel(key = "id")]
    todos: Signal<Vec<Todo>>,              // signal 0
    filter: Signal<Filter>,                // signal 1
    visible: Computed<Vec<Todo>>,          // signal 2, derived
    remaining: Computed<u32>,              // signal 3, derived
}

#[keel::api(store)]
impl Todos {
    pub fn new(ctx: Ctx) -> Self { /* … */ }
    pub async fn add(&self, title: String) -> Result<Todo, TodoError> { /* … */ }
    pub fn toggle(&self, id: Uuid) { /* … */ }
    pub fn set_filter(&self, filter: Filter) { self.filter.set(filter); }
}
```

A few rules worth knowing up front:

- **Signals are the fields of type `Signal<T>` and `Computed<T>`**, numbered in declaration order (0, 1, 2, …). Other fields are private state: a `Ctx`, a counter, configuration.
- **A store needs a constructor**, a `pub fn` returning `Self` or `Result<Self, E>`. Generated code calls it to create the object in the core and gets back a handle.
- **Receivers are `&self`.** Objects are shared, so mutation goes through signals or a lock. `&mut self` is rejected with a teaching error (`E0020`).
- **Method arguments and results are wire types**: numbers, strings, bytes, options, vectors, maps, your records and enums, and `Result<T, E>` where `E` is a `#[keel::error]` enum.

## Signals

A `Signal<T>` holds a value. You read it with `get()` (a clone) or `with(|v| …)` (a borrow), and write it with `set(value)` or `update(|v| …)`.

rust

```rust
self.filter.set(Filter::Done);                       // replace
self.todos.update(|list| list.retain(|t| !t.done));  // edit in place
let open = self.todos.with(|list| list.iter().filter(|t| !t.done).count());
```

A write outside a transaction is an implicit single-write transaction, so the change is committed and delivered at once. Inside `update`, the closure holds the value's write lock: it must not read or write the same signal, or read a computed derived from it. A violation panics with a clear message instead of deadlocking.

## Computeds

A `Computed<T>` is a value derived from signals. You name its inputs and give it a function of them:

rust

```rust
let visible = Computed::new((&todos, &filter), |(todos, filter)| {
    todos.iter().filter(|t| filter.matches(t)).cloned().collect()
});
let remaining = Computed::new(&todos, |todos| todos.iter().filter(|t| !t.done).count() as u32);
```

Inputs are `&Signal<A>` or `&Computed<A>`, or a tuple of up to six of them, and the closure receives references. A computed is recomputed in the core, in dependency order, and **pushed in the same change-set as the write that caused it**. The UI never derives anything itself, so it cannot disagree with the core about, say, how many items are left.

Because a store with computeds cannot be rebuilt from its plain signals automatically, you name a function that assembles it: `#[keel::store(restore = "Self::assemble")]`. The macro tells you when you forget (`E0013`).

## Transactions

When several signals change together, group the writes. Everything inside `ctx.txn` commits as one transaction, so observers see one consistent change-set and never a half-applied state. The playground's counter changes two signals and derives a third:

core/src/counter.rs

```rust
pub fn add(&self, amount: i32) {
    self.ctx.txn(|| {
        self.count.update(|c| *c = c.saturating_add(amount));
        self.changes.update(|n| *n = n.saturating_add(1));
    });   // one change-set carries count, changes and parity
}
```

Transactions nest: an inner `txn` joins the outer one. A change-set is never split, and change-sets are delivered in commit order; for one store they reach the platform one at a time with strictly increasing transaction ids.

## Change-sets and observation

A platform does not receive everything. It **observes** signals, and only observed signals that changed are sent. Two details follow from that:

- **Observing sends the current value right away**, before the call returns in-process, so a store's initial state arrives as an ordinary change-set. A signal written while unobserved is remembered as pending and sent when someone starts observing it.
- **Only what changed is sent.** Writing `filter` in the to-do store ships `filter` and the recomputed `visible`, and nothing else, because `todos` did not change.

A signal marked `#[keel(no_coalesce)]` is delivered on every commit instead of being folded into the latest value. A change-set is a compact binary structure, described on the [architecture page](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/architecture.html#the-wire).

For side effects that belong in the core, `Effect::new(deps, f)` runs `f` after each commit that dirtied one of its dependencies, and is cancelled when dropped.

## Keyed lists

A `Signal<Vec<T>>` marked `#[keel(key = "field")]` is a **keyed list**. The key is the identity of a row, and the core sends changes to it as a patch of positional operations instead of the whole list.

| Operation | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Insert { index, item }` | put the item at `index` |
| `Remove { index }` | take the row at `index` out |
| `Update { index, item }` | replace the row at `index` |
| `Move { from, to }` | take the row at `from`, then place it so it ends at `to` |
| `Clear` | empty the list |

The platform applies the operations in order to its own copy of the list. If a patch ever disagrees with that copy (an index out of bounds), the platform treats the signal as out of sync and observes it again, which resends the full value.

### Why a list write costs the change, not the list

How the core produces the patch decides the cost. There are two ways.

**Recorded operations** are the fast path. `Signal<Vec<T>>` has `push`, `insert`, `remove`, `update_at`, `move_item` and `clear`. Each one mutates the list and appends the operation it performed to a log; at commit, that log *is* the patch. No key is hashed and no item is compared, so the cost is the change, not the length of the list.

examples/playground/core/src/biglist.rs

```rust
/// Inserts a new row so that it ends at `index`. One keyed `Insert`.
pub fn insert_at(&self, index: u32, label: String) -> Result<u32, ListError> {
    // …check the index…
    let id = self.next_id.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
    self.items.insert(index as usize, Item { id, label, version: 0 });
    Ok(id)
}
```

**Raw writes** (`set`, `update`, `replace`) are the fallback. They are always correct, but the core cannot know what you did, so at commit it diffs the new list against what the platform has: hash every key, compare the surviving rows. That is O(list). It also falls back to sending the whole value when the two lists share no key, a key occurs twice, or more than half of the old rows were removed.

The difference is measured. On a 10,000-row observed list, median times from the benchmark suite (host-measured, Apple M5 Pro):

| One change to 10,000 rows | Diffed | Recorded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Insert | 536.16 µs | **6.31 µs** |
| Update | 532.32 µs | **272.3 ns** |
| Move | 702.95 µs | **9.74 µs** |

What remains at 10,000 rows is the memory move of the vector's tail, which `Vec::insert` needs in the core and which is paid twice (the list and its baseline): about 0.6 ns per row. The same insert into 100 rows is 359 ns and into 1,000 rows is 770 ns. The decision record is [ADR-027](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-027-keyed-list-ops-are-recorded-not-diffed.md).

**Rule of thumb.** Inside a store, reach for `push`, `insert`, `remove`, `update_at` and `move_item` when you change one row. Use `set` or `update` when you genuinely replace the list (a refresh from the server) or make an edit no recorded operation can express. A transaction that mixes both is diffed as a whole.

## What the platforms see

Each platform runtime holds a **mirror**: store handle, then signal id, then the decoded value. Generated code exposes the mirror in the platform's own idiom (an `@Observable` property, a `StateFlow`, a `Signal` with `useSignal`), so reading is a local memory read that never calls into the core.

Change-sets are applied on the main thread with per-frame coalescing: Swift on the `MainActor`, Kotlin on `Dispatchers.Main.immediate`, and TypeScript by batching into one flush per macrotask. A store is an object with a lifetime: release it explicitly with `close()` (Swift and Kotlin use `deinit` and a `Cleaner` as backstops, TypeScript a `FinalizationRegistry`), and `KeelCore.stats()` shows live handle counts.

## Snapshot and restore

The core can snapshot every store's plain signals (computeds are left out and recomputed) and restore them, which is how a web page recovers after a crash and how tests rebuild state. Restore keeps the same handles valid, so the platform's references keep working, and it cancels calls that were running on the stores it replaced. This is why the `restore` function above rebuilds computeds from signals, and why the to-do store continues its id counter above the largest id in the snapshot.

## Determinism

The core reads no clock and no random source and starts no thread of its own. Time comes from the `Clock` port, delays from `ctx.sleep` (which goes through the `Timer` port), randomness from `Rng`, the network from `Http`. That is rule R12, and it is why every scenario can be driven with deterministic fakes in Rust and with in-memory adapters on each platform. The to-do store's ids come from a counter for the same reason. See [Ports & adapters](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/ports.html).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/queries.html

# Queries & mutations

Data fetching, caching and offline behaviour are not something each platform reimplements. They live in the core, next to the state they feed, and every platform observes the same cache.

## Why the data layer is in the core

Fetching, caching, retrying, optimistic updates and offline queues are logic, and logic is what Keel writes once. The core never opens a socket: every request goes through the `Http` port, which is `URLSession`, OkHttp or `fetch` in an app and a scripted fake in a test. The query client keeps one cache that all platforms observe, so the to-do list on the iPhone and the one in a Chrome tab agree about what is fresh.

## Defining a query

A query is an `async fn` whose first parameter is the `Ctx`, marked with `#[keel::query]`. This is the playground's remote to-do list, a `GET` that is cached per list:

core/src/remote.rs

```rust
/// The items of the server's list `list`: `GET {base}/lists/{list}/todos`.
#[keel::query(key = "remote-todos:{list}", stale = "30s", persist, retry = 1)]
pub async fn remote_todos(ctx: &Ctx, list: String) -> Result<Vec<RemoteTodo>, RemoteError> {
    let url = endpoint(ctx, &format!("/lists/{list}/todos"))?;
    parse(&send(ctx, HttpRequest::get(url)).await?)
}
```

| Argument | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `key = "…"` | the cache key; `{param}` placeholders name parameters, so two lists are two independent entries |
| `stale = "30s"` | how long a successful result stays fresh |
| `persist` | write the entry to the `Kv` port so it survives a restart |
| `retry = 3` | how many times to retry a failed fetch |
| `idempotent` | (mutations) the request is safe to repeat, which makes it eligible for the offline queue |

The signature is checked when you compile: it must be `async`, take `ctx: &Ctx` first, and return `Result<T, E>`. A query whose success value is `()` or an `Option` is rejected, because a query caches a value and effects belong in a mutation (`E0040` to `E0042`).

## Observing a query

Platforms observe a query through a generated **query handle**, which is an ordinary store. For `remote_todos` it is `RemoteTodosQueryHandle`, and it has five signals:

| Signal | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `data` | the latest successful result, or nothing yet |
| `status` | `idle`, `fetching`, `success` or `error` |
| `error` | the error of the latest failed fetch, cleared by the next success |
| `fetching` | whether a request is in flight, also true while refetching stale data |
| `updatedAt` | when `data` last changed |

Constructing the handle registers an observer and starts a fetch if the entry is missing or stale. Releasing it removes the observer; when the last observer goes, the in-flight fetch is cancelled and the entry is kept for five minutes before it is garbage collected. The handle also has `refetch()` (fetch now, even if fresh) and `invalidate()` (mark stale; it refetches while observed).

tsx

```tsx
const inbox = await RemoteTodosQueryHandle.create("inbox");   // observe
const items = useSignal(inbox.data);                          // in a component
const busy = useSignal(inbox.fetching);
```

## Staleness, refetch and dedup

An observed entry refetches when it is stale and something happens:

- an observer is added while it is stale,
- the app becomes `Active` again (the `Lifecycle` port),
- connectivity returns (the `Connectivity` port),
- its optional interval elapses, or
- it is invalidated, by key prefix.

**One fetch per key at a time.** If five screens observe the same list, they share one in-flight request.

## Retry with jitter

A failed fetch is retried `retry` times (three by default) with exponential backoff, `min(1000 × 2ⁿ, 30000)` milliseconds, with plus or minus 20% jitter. The jitter comes from the `Rng` port and the delay from the `Timer` port, so a test with fakes sees exactly the schedule it scripts.

## Mutations

A mutation is an `async fn` marked `#[keel::mutation]`. It shares its cache key with the query it affects. Call it through the context:

rust

```rust
ctx.mutate::<PostRemoteTodoMutation>((list, title))
    .optimistic(move |cache| {
        cache.update::<RemoteTodosQuery>((cached,), |items| items.push(placeholder));
    })
    .invalidates(/* keys to mark stale */)
    .await
```

`optimistic` runs inside a transaction with typed access to cache entries (`get`, `set`, `update`), so the UI shows the new item at once. On success the `invalidates` keys are marked stale and refetched if observed, which replaces the placeholder with the server's item. The playground wraps this in `create_remote_todo` and `set_remote_done`, which are what its three UIs call.

### Precise rollback

If the mutation fails, the optimistic write is undone, but only **the writes that mutation made**. Every cache entry carries a write stamp that changes with each write: an optimistic write, a `set`, or a fetch result. When a mutation fails, each entry it wrote is restored to what it was before, *unless something else has written that entry since*. An entry that was written since keeps that write.

That rule is what makes concurrent mutations safe:

- a later optimistic mutation's placeholder survives an earlier mutation's rollback, even on the same entry;
- a fetch result that arrived in the meantime is newer than the failed closure and is kept;
- a later mutation that wrote directly on top of the failed one inherits its restore point, so if it fails too the entry goes back to before both.

Stamps are compared, never contents, so two writes of equal data are still distinguishable. This behaviour is covered by the optimistic-rollback contract scenario on all three platforms.

## The offline queue

A mutation marked `idempotent` that fails with a network error while the `Connectivity` port says the device is offline is not lost. It is appended to a persisted queue (the `Kv` key `keel.query.queue`) with its parameters and an idempotency key, and replayed in order when connectivity returns. The request carries an `Idempotency-Key` header that stays the same across retries and replays, so a server can tell a repeat from a second item.

rust

```rust
#[keel::mutation(key = "remote-todos:{list}", idempotent)]
pub async fn post_remote_todo(ctx: &Ctx, list: String, title: String) -> Result<RemoteTodo, RemoteError> {
    // …
    if let Some(key) = keel::query::idempotency_key() {
        request = request.with_header("Idempotency-Key", key.to_string());
    }
    // …
}
```

A mutation that is not `idempotent` fails immediately when offline. While a queued call waits, the optimistic placeholder stays visible, and the caller's `await` keeps waiting until the network returns and the request is replayed.

## Persistence

Entries marked `persist` are written to the `Kv` port after each successful fetch (debounced, 250 ms) and read back when the core starts. Each entry stores the schema hash it was written under, and an entry from a different schema is dropped rather than decoded wrongly.

## Testing without a network

Because the network is a port, a query is tested with a scripted fake and no sockets. `FakeHttp` answers from rules and records every request, including a flaky endpoint:

rust

```rust
let http = FakeHttp::new();
// two timeouts, then success for ever after
http.respond_sequence("https://x.test/a", [Err(HttpError::Timeout), Err(HttpError::Timeout)]);
http.respond("https://x.test/a", HttpResponse::new(200, b"ok".to_vec()));
```

Pair it with `FakeClock` to advance time and `ScriptedConnectivity` to go offline. [Ports & adapters](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/ports.html) lists them all.

## See it run

The playground's **Remote** tab on every platform is this page in motion: a cached query, optimistic adds that roll back when the server refuses, and an **Offline** switch that queues writes and replays them on reconnect. Its source is [`examples/playground/core/src/remote.rs`](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/examples/playground/core/src/remote.rs).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/ports.html

# Ports & adapters

The core never touches the outside world directly. Time, randomness, the network, storage and the app's lifecycle all come through ports: traits the platform implements and the core calls.

## What a port is

A port is a Rust trait marked `#[keel::port]`. The platform implements it (an adapter), or a Rust fake does in a test. The core calls it through the context, for example `ctx.http().request(req).await`, and does not know or care what is behind it. That is what keeps the core deterministic (rule R12): it has no wall clock, no random source and no threads outside the `Clock`, `Rng` and `Timer` ports and the runtime.

There are three kinds, and the kind decides how a call travels:

| Kind | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **sync** | the platform answers before the call returns. A port is sync only if every method is sync |
| **async** | the platform answers later; the core's task waits, and can be cancelled |
| **event** | fire and forget from the platform into the core, such as "connectivity changed" |

## The ten standard ports

| Port | Kind | Methods |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Clock` | sync | `now_ms() -> i64`, `monotonic_ns() -> u64` |
| `Rng` | sync | `fill(len) -> Bytes` |
| `Log` | sync | `log(level, target, message)` |
| `Http` | async | `request(HttpRequest) -> Result<HttpResponse, HttpError>` |
| `Kv` | async | `get`, `set`, `delete`, `list(prefix)` |
| `SecureStore` | async | the same shape as `Kv`, for secrets |
| `Fs` | async | `read`, `write`, `delete`, `list`, each returning `Result<_, FsError>` |
| `Timer` | sync | `set(timer_id, delay_ms)`; the platform answers later with a timer-fired event |
| `Connectivity` | event | `changed(online, kind)` with `NetKind` of `Wifi`, `Cellular`, `Wired`, `Unknown` or `None` |
| `Lifecycle` | event | `changed(state)` with `AppState` of `Active`, `Inactive` or `Background` |

They exchange a small set of types: `HttpRequest` (method, url, headers, optional body, optional timeout), `HttpResponse` (status, headers, body), `HttpError` (`Network`, `Timeout`, `Cancelled`, `InvalidUrl`), `Header`, `FsError` (`NotFound`, `Denied`, `Io`), `NetKind` and `AppState`.

These ports and types ship inside each platform runtime and are **not** generated into your app's bindings. Every core links `keel-ports`, so its schema contains them and the schema hash covers them, but the generator leaves them out and the generated code refers to the runtime's own types. That is why your app can have its own record called `Timer` or `Log`.

## Default adapters

Each runtime ships an adapter for every port, so a new app works without adapter code.

| Port | Swift | Kotlin (Android) | TypeScript (browser) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Http` | `URLSession` | `OkHttp` (optional dependency) or `HttpURLConnection` | `fetch` |
| `Kv` | files in Application Support | `SharedPreferences`-backed files | IndexedDB |
| `SecureStore` | Keychain | `EncryptedFile` (Keystore) | IndexedDB with WebCrypto |
| `Fs` | `FileManager` | `Context.filesDir` | OPFS |
| `Clock`, `Rng`, `Log` | Foundation, `SecRandom`, `os_log` | `System`, `SecureRandom`, `Log` | built in |
| `Timer` | `DispatchQueue` | `Handler`, `ScheduledExecutor` | `setTimeout` |
| `Connectivity`, `Lifecycle` | `NWPathMonitor`, `scenePhase` | `ConnectivityManager`, `ProcessLifecycleOwner` | `navigator.onLine`, `visibilitychange` |

On the JVM without Android, `Connectivity` and `Lifecycle` are stubs. On the web, `Clock`, `Rng` and `Log` are bound to imports of the wasm module, so a web app needs no adapter code for them.

## Supplying your own adapter

You replace a default when you load the core. The playground replaces `Http` with an in-memory server (so it needs no backend) and `Kv` with a map:

web/src/keel.ts

```ts
const adapters = { http: server, kv: memoryKv() };
await KeelCore.load({
  mode: "wasm-main",
  wasm: new URL(wasmUrl, location.href),
  expectedSchemaHash: KeelIds.schemaHash,
  adapters,
});
```

ios/PlaygroundApp/KeelBootstrap.swift

```swift
let adapters = Adapters.platformDefault
    .removing(portId: fnv1a32("port.Connectivity"))
    .replacing(PlaygroundNetwork.shared)
    .replacing(KvAdapter(directory: store))
try KeelCore.load(.inproc(adapters: adapters, expectedSchemaHash: KeelIds.schemaHash))
```

android/.../KeelApp.kt

```kotlin
KeelCore.load(
    LoadOptions(
        expectedSchemaHash = KeelIds.SCHEMA_HASH,
        adapters = mapOf(
            StandardPorts.Http.PORT_ID to server.portImpl(),
            StandardPorts.Kv.PORT_ID to InMemoryKv().portImpl(),
        ),
    ),
)
```

Register the ports your core needs at load time. A core's start-up work (query hydration reads the `Kv` port) runs as soon as the runtime exists, so a port registered later can be missed by that work.

## When a port is missing

An unavailable port is a normal outcome, not a bug. A port nobody registered behaves as unavailable, a call can be cancelled, and a host can reply with bytes that do not decode. The core handles all three without panicking:

- If the port method returns `Result<T, E>`, the failure becomes an `E`. `HttpError` and `FsError` implement `From<PortError>`, so an unavailable `Http` port is `Network("the Http port has no adapter registered")`. Your own error type needs the same conversion, and the macro checks it at compile time (`E0033`).
- If the method has no error channel, there is no typed way to say "unavailable", so the call panics with a message that names the port and method and says how to bind one (`E0062`). The runtime contains that panic at the boundary. Give optional ports a `Result`, or register them.

## Writing your own port

Mark a trait with `#[keel::port]`. The macro registers it in the schema and generates a proxy type, so the core calls your trait like any other, and the platform gets a protocol or interface to implement. This one is made up, to show the shape:

rust

```rust
#[keel::port(sync)]
pub trait Haptics {
    fn tap(&self, strength: u8);
}
```

A port method's parameters must be wire types (`E0030`), and an `event` port's methods cannot return a value (`E0031`).

## Testing with fakes

Every standard port has a deterministic Rust fake in `keel::ports::fakes`. They are all `Send + Sync`, keep state behind a lock, and never read the system clock, a random source or a thread.

| Fake | Port | Behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FakeHttp` | `Http` | scripted replies chosen by a matcher; every request recorded |
| `MemKv`, `MemSecureStore` | `Kv`, `SecureStore` | in-memory ordered maps; operations recorded |
| `MemFs` | `Fs` | in-memory tree with the platform adapters' error semantics |
| `FakeClock` | `Clock` and `Timer` | settable time; `advance` fires due timers |
| `SeededRng` | `Rng` | `xorshift64*`; the same seed gives the same bytes |
| `CaptureLog` | `Log` | keeps every record |
| `ScriptedConnectivity`, `ScriptedLifecycle` | `Connectivity`, `Lifecycle` | push scripted events into a runtime |

`TestRuntime::new()` runs the executor on the test thread and lets you drive it with `run_until(fut)` and `run_pending()`. Installing the fakes binds all of them into it. The doctest of `FakeHttp` shows the style:

rust

```rust
use keel_ports::{Http, HttpError, HttpRequest, HttpResponse};
use keel_ports::fakes::FakeHttp;
use keel_runtime::testing::TestRuntime;

let http = FakeHttp::new();
// A flaky endpoint: two timeouts, then success for ever after.
http.respond_sequence("https://x.test/a", [Err(HttpError::Timeout), Err(HttpError::Timeout)]);
http.respond("https://x.test/a", HttpResponse::new(200, b"ok".to_vec()));

let t = TestRuntime::new();
let get = || HttpRequest::get("https://x.test/a");
assert_eq!(t.run_until(http.request(get())), Err(HttpError::Timeout));
assert_eq!(t.run_until(http.request(get())), Err(HttpError::Timeout));
assert_eq!(t.run_until(http.request(get())).unwrap().status, 200);
assert_eq!(http.call_count(), 3);
```

Time works the same way. `FakeClock` is the single source of time for both `Clock` and `Timer`, so `ctx.sleep` asks for a timer and advancing the fake clock serves it: sleeps wake at exactly their deadline. On a runtime with the fakes installed, advance time with `Fakes::advance`, not `TestRuntime::advance`.

The platforms get the same treatment. The [contract scenarios](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/contract-tests/scenarios.md) run every platform runtime against the real core with a manual clock, an in-memory `Http` server, an in-memory `Kv` and a test that emits connectivity events itself.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/cli.html

# The CLI

One binary runs the whole loop: scaffold a project, generate bindings, build the core for each platform, serve it live, and check your machine. Every command teaches through its own help.

## Overview

text

```
keel [-C <dir>] <command>

  init      create a new project: a core crate and an app shell per platform
  bindgen   generate Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript bindings from the core's schema
  build     build the core for iOS, Android, the web or this machine
  dev       serve the core over a WebSocket to running apps, rebuilding on change
  doctor    check toolchains and SDKs against what the project needs
  adopt     add a Keel core to an existing app, without touching its project files
```

A Keel project is a directory with a `keel.toml`. Commands find it from the current directory upwards, or you can point at it with the global `-C <dir>` (long form `--project-dir`). `keel <command> --help` prints what the command does, what it needs, what it writes, and examples.

Exit status is `0` on success, `1` for a failed command or a failed `keel doctor`, and `2` for a bad command line.

## keel init

bash

```bash
keel init todo                              # all three platforms
keel init todo --platforms ios,web          # only those shells
keel init todo --id dev.acme.todo           # application id / bundle identifier
keel init todo --keel-path ~/src/keel       # use a local checkout of Keel
```

Creates a project directory with `keel.toml`, `core/` (a working to-do store), `generated/` (bindings, already generated) and one minimal, real app per platform in `ios/`, `android/` and `web/`. Nothing is downloaded: the templates are part of the binary. Without `--keel-path` the project depends on released versions of the crates and runtimes.

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `<name>` | project name: letters, digits, `-` and `_` |
| `--platforms <list>` | `ios`, `android`, `web`, comma separated; default all three (alias `--targets`) |
| `--id <id>` | application id and iOS bundle identifier; default `com.example.<name>` |
| `--keel-path <dir>` | use the crates and runtimes of a Keel checkout (or set `KEEL_PATH`) |
| `--dir <dir>` | create the project inside this directory instead of the current one |

## keel bindgen

bash

```bash
keel bindgen                          # build the core, extract the schema, write <project>/generated
keel bindgen --out ../shared/bindings
keel bindgen --schema schema.json     # no build: generate from a schema file
keel bindgen --check                  # exit 1 if the generated files are stale (for CI)
keel bindgen --docs                   # include the core's doc comments
```

Reads the core's schema and writes the bindings the app shells import: a Swift package (`<out>/swift/`), a Gradle module (`<out>/kotlin/`) and an npm package (`<out>/ts/`). By default the schema comes from the core itself: the core is built as a host library, loaded, and asked for its schema. With `--schema` it is read from a file instead and nothing is built. Files an earlier run wrote and this one does not are removed; files you added next to them are never touched.

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--schema <file>` | generate from this schema JSON instead of building the core |
| `--out <dir>` | write below this directory (default `[paths] generated` in `keel.toml`) |
| `--release` | extract the schema from a release build of the core |
| `--platforms <list>` | only these platforms' bindings (`ios` is Swift, `android` is Kotlin, `web` is TypeScript) |
| `--check` | write nothing; exit with an error if the generated files differ from what would be written |
| `--docs` | keep the core's doc comments in the bindings |
| `--crate-name <name>` | the core crate's name, for a schema file that has none |

The schema a library exports is the canonical form its hash is computed from, and that form has no doc comments. `--docs` runs the core once more to read the full schema so the generated code carries the same documentation as the Rust source.

## keel build

bash

```bash
keel build                                   # every platform in keel.toml, debug
keel build --release                         # optimized: what you ship
keel build --platform web --release
keel build --platform android,host
```

Builds the core for each platform and puts the result where the app shells look for it, below `build/`:

| Target | Output |
| --- | --- |
| `ios` | `build/ios/KeelCore.xcframework`, device and simulator slices |
| `android` | `build/android/jniLibs/<abi>/libkeel_core.so`, arm64-v8a and x86_64, 16 KB page aligned |
| `web` | `build/web/keel_core.wasm`, release profile, then `wasm-opt -Oz` if installed |
| `host` | `build/host/libkeel_core.{dylib,so}`, for the JVM tests and `keel bindgen` |

`--release` turns on LTO and one codegen unit. The web build is always optimized. Sizes are printed at the end next to the design's budgets. A debug Android core is tens of megabytes per ABI, so package with `--release`. The library is your core plus the Keel C ABI, built from a small crate generated under `target/keel/`; you never write that crate.

**iOS debug builds.** Link the library with `-force_load` (the generated Xcode project already does), or the core's registrations are dropped by the linker and the schema is empty. Release builds need no flag.

## keel dev

bash

```bash
keel dev                          # listen on 127.0.0.1:7443
keel dev --addr 0.0.0.0:7443      # reachable from a phone on your network
keel dev --no-watch               # build once and serve
```

Runs the core on this machine and serves it over a WebSocket. A simulator, a phone or a browser tab connects with the `remote` transport and uses this core instead of a built-in one: edit Rust, save, the core is rebuilt and restarted, reload the app to reconnect. Logs, including the development records (a line per transaction commit, port call and panic), print here. Clocks, randomness and logging are answered by this machine, because a remote client cannot answer a synchronous port.

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--addr <addr>` | address to listen on; port 0 picks a free one (default `127.0.0.1:7443`) |
| `--no-watch` | build once and serve; do not rebuild on change |
| `--log-level <n>` | log records below this level (0 trace to 5 fatal) are not printed; default 1 |

How each platform connects:

| Platform | How |
| --- | --- |
| Web | `KeelCore.load({ mode: "remote", url: "ws://127.0.0.1:7443", expectedSchemaHash })` |
| iOS | set `KEEL_DEV_URL=ws://<your Mac>:7443`; the generated app reads it in debug builds |
| Android | the Kotlin runtime has no remote transport on Android yet; use the JVM or the web |

**No authentication.** The server has none. Keep the loopback default unless a device has to reach it.

## keel doctor

bash

```bash
keel doctor
keel doctor --platform ios
```

Checks what the platforms need and prints one line per finding with the fix for each gap: Rust and its targets, Xcode (and whether `xcode-select` points at it), the Android SDK, NDK and `cargo-ndk`, Node, `wasm-opt` and a JDK. Inside a project only the platforms named in `keel.toml` are checked; elsewhere it checks all of them. It exits with status 1 when something the project needs is missing.

## keel adopt

bash

```bash
keel adopt ../MyApp                          # detect platforms, write ../MyApp/keel/
keel adopt . --platform ios                  # only the iOS steps
keel adopt ../MyApp --keel-path ~/src/keel   # use a local checkout of Keel
```

Adds a Keel core to an app you already have, the conservative way. It writes one new `keel/` directory (a core crate, a `keel.toml` and a `KEEL_ADOPT.md`) and a list of the exact steps to wire it into the app, with the paths already filled in. The app's own project files are never modified; you make the few edits yourself.

It detects iOS from `*.xcodeproj` or `Package.swift`, Android from `settings.gradle(.kts)` plus `AndroidManifest.xml`, and web from a `package.json` (Vite, webpack, Next and so on). Flags: `--platform <list>`, `--name <name>` (the core's name; default the directory's name) and `--keel-path <dir>`.

## keel.toml

`keel init` writes every setting that matters, with comments.

keel.toml

```toml
[project]
name = "todo"
id = "com.example.todo"        # Android applicationId, iOS bundle id, Kotlin package base
platforms = ["ios", "android", "web"]

[core]
path = "core"                  # the crate bindgen, build and dev work on

[paths]
generated = "generated"        # written by `keel bindgen`; commit it or check it in CI
build = "build"                # written by `keel build`; do not commit

[keel]
version = "0.1"                # path = "…" points at a checkout of the Keel repository

[bindings]
# swift_module = "TodoCore"
# kotlin_package = "com.example.todo.core"
# ts_scope = "app"
# ts_js_number = false         # i64/u64 as `number` instead of `bigint`
# swift_typed_throws = true    # `throws(E)`; false emits plain `throws`
```

Commit `generated/` or regenerate it in CI, and gate on `keel bindgen --check` so a stale binding cannot ship.

## Errors

CLI errors print as `error[keel::C00NN]` with what happened, why, and what to do. Macro errors in your Rust use the same teaching shape with `E00NN` codes; the catalogue is on the [architecture page](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/architecture.html#diagnostics).

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/architecture.html

# Architecture

One schema feeds three generators. Three runtimes hold the mirrors. A small binary wire carries writes in and change-sets out. This page is the tour, and the specification in the repository is the contract.

## The shape of it

Keel is a Rust core, a schema extracted from it, three code generators, and three platform runtimes. Your screens sit on generated bindings; the bindings sit on a runtime package; the runtime talks to the core through a transport that is an ABI, not a framework.

*Figure: Each platform has the same four layers; only the bottom one is platform-specific machinery.*

The core is one codebase. On each platform it is linked the way that platform expects: a static library in an XCFramework on iOS, `libkeel_core.so` over JNI on Android, a wasm module on the web. During development the same core can instead run on your machine behind a WebSocket (`keel dev`).

## From Rust to native code

*Figure: Everything is derived from the schema. Bindgen emits three trees that depend only on the matching runtime package.*

Everything starts with the macros. `#[keel::api]`, `#[keel::store]`, `#[keel::port]` and friends validate your code and register a description of each public type and function. Collected together, those descriptions are the **schema**: records, enums, objects, stores with their signals, functions, ports and queries. The CLI builds your core as a host library, loads it, asks for the schema, and hands it to `keel bindgen`, which writes a Swift package, a Gradle module and an npm package. Generated code depends only on the matching runtime package.

Three properties of this design are worth stating plainly:

- **Names become ids at compile time.** A type id is a hash of its name, a method id a hash of `Type.method`, a port id a hash of `port.Trait`, and a signal id is its position among the store's signal fields. Every platform agrees without a registry lookup. The hash is FNV-1a.
- **The schema has a hash.** It is the FNV-1a hash of a canonical form: lists sorted by name, no whitespace, doc comments excluded, so two cores with the same public surface hash the same. Each binding carries the hash it was generated from, and the runtime compares it with the core's when it attaches.
- **Generated code is reviewed like hand-written code.** Golden files lock the output for all three languages, and the output is compiled and run in tests. A record becomes a Swift `struct`, a Kotlin `data class` and a TypeScript `interface`; an error becomes a typed-`throws` enum, a sealed class and an `Error` subclass. See the API overviews for [Swift](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/api-swift.html), [Kotlin](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/api-kotlin.html) and [TypeScript](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/api-typescript.html).

The standard ports and their types are in every schema but are not generated into your bindings, because each runtime already implements them; see [Ports & adapters](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/ports.html).

## The crates

Twelve Rust crates, and only one of them may contain `unsafe`.

| Crate | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `keel-meta` | the schema model, canonical JSON, the hash, the FNV helpers and registration |
| `keel-wire` | the binary codec, envelope and patches; no `unsafe`, proptested and byte-fuzzed |
| `keel-macros` | the attribute macros and their teaching diagnostics |
| `keel-signals` | `Signal`, `Computed`, `Effect`, transactions, change-set building, keyed patches |
| `keel-runtime` | the executor, core lock, object table, ports, timers, snapshots and panic guard |
| `keel-ports` | the ten standard ports, their records and the deterministic fakes |
| `keel-query` | the query client, mutations, retry, persistence and the offline queue |
| `keel-ffi` | the C ABI, the JNI shim and the wasm exports: **the only `unsafe`** |
| `keel-transport` | the WebSocket server and framing behind `keel dev` |
| `keel-bindgen` | the Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript generators |
| `keel-cli` | the `keel` command |
| `keel` | the facade you depend on: prelude, macros, runtime, ports, query |

The runtimes are `runtimes/swift/KeelRuntime`, `runtimes/kotlin/keel-runtime` and `runtimes/ts/@keel/runtime`. The Kotlin runtime depends on the standard library and kotlinx-coroutines only, and the TypeScript core package has no runtime dependencies.

## The wire

The wire is small on purpose. It is little-endian throughout, with no alignment and no padding. All lengths are `u32`. Decoders never panic on malformed input; they return a typed error.

| Type | Encoding |
| --- | --- |
| integers, floats | fixed width, two's complement or IEEE 754 |
| `bool` | one byte, 0 or 1 (other values are rejected) |
| `String`, `Bytes` | `u32` length, then the bytes (strings validated as UTF-8) |
| `Option<T>` | a tag byte, then the value if present |
| `Vec<T>` | `u32` count, then the items |
| `Map<K, V>` | `u32` count, then pairs, sorted by encoded key so the bytes are deterministic |
| `Duration`, `Timestamp` | `i64` nanoseconds, `i64` milliseconds since the Unix epoch |
| `Uuid` | 16 raw bytes |
| record | its fields in declaration order |
| enum, error | `u16` variant index, then that variant's fields |
| `Result<T, E>` | a tag byte, then `T` or `E` |
| object handle | `u64`: low 32 bits slot, high 32 bits generation |

Transports that cross a real pipe (the WebSocket and worker transports) wrap every message in a 23-byte envelope. In-process calls skip it and carry only the payload.

*Figure: The envelope frames every message on the WebSocket and worker transports. In-process calls carry only the payload.*

The `kind` byte says what the payload is:

| Kind | Name | Direction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1, 2 | Call, Reply | host to core, core to host |
| 3 | ChangeSet | core to host |
| 4, 5 | PortCall, PortReply | core to host, host to core |
| 6, 7 | Cancel, StreamCredit | host to core |
| 8 | StreamItem | core to host |
| 9, 10 | Observe, Release | host to core |
| 11 | Event | host to core (connectivity, lifecycle) |
| 12 | Hello | both: Keel version, schema hash, platform, mode |
| 13 | Log | core to host |
| 14 | TimerFired | host to core |
| 15, 16 | Snapshot, Restore | core to host, host to core |

A **call** carries a target (free function, object method, constructor or lazy page), the object handle, the method id, a call id the host chose, and the arguments encoded in order. The **reply** carries the call id and a status: `0` ok, `1` a typed error, `2` a panic (message and backtrace), `3` cancelled, `4` a stream was opened, `5` a bad request such as an unknown method or a schema mismatch. A failure is always a typed value; nothing escapes as an abort.

A **change-set** is how state comes back. It carries a transaction id and one entry per dirty observed signal.

*Figure: Entries are ordered by signal id. A keyed patch inside an entry is a count and a list of operations.*

An entry's `op` is `0` for a full value, `1` for a keyed patch, and `2` for "lazy list invalidated". A keyed patch is a count and a list of operations (`Insert`, `Remove`, `Update`, `Move`, `Clear`) applied in order to the host's copy; see [Core concepts](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/concepts.html#keyed-lists). The `len` field lets a host skip an entry it cannot decode.

**Streams** use credit-based backpressure. A host grants credit and the core sends at most that many items beyond what has been credited; generated bindings grant 16 on subscribe and top up when consumption drops below 8. A cancel closes the stream.

## The boundary

The native boundary is a C ABI, exported with `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` and nothing but C-compatible types. The whole surface is nineteen functions (parameter lists abridged here):

c

```c
uint32_t keel_abi_version(void);
uint64_t keel_schema_hash(void);
KeelBuf  keel_schema_json(void);
uint32_t keel_init(cfg, len, reply_cb, changeset_cb, stream_cb, user);
void     keel_shutdown(void);
uint32_t keel_call(ptr, len);          // async reply arrives on reply_cb
KeelBuf  keel_call_sync(ptr, len);     // reply returned directly
void     keel_cancel(call_id);
void     keel_stream_credit(call_id, credit);
void     keel_observe(handle, signal_id, on);
void     keel_release(handle);
void     keel_port_register(port_id, cb, user);
void     keel_port_reply(ptr, len);
void     keel_event(port_id, method_id, ptr, len);
void     keel_timer_fired(timer_id);
KeelBuf  keel_snapshot(void);
uint32_t keel_restore(ptr, len);
KeelBuf  keel_stats_json(void);
void     keel_buf_free(KeelBuf buf);
```

Android reaches the same functions through a JNI shim that registers its natives once at load, so there is no per-call lookup. The web has no wasm-bindgen: the module exports and imports use only `i32`, `i64` and `f64`, a 64-bit handle is passed as two halves, and `keel_poll()` drives the executor. `Clock`, `Rng` and `Log` are bound to wasm imports, so a web app needs no adapter code for them.

Callbacks are where hosts get hurt, so the contract is explicit and enforced. A callback runs on whichever thread produced the event, possibly with the core lock held, so it must be short, thread-safe and must not throw. It must not call back into the core except the few entries that never take the lock (freeing a buffer, replying to a port call, granting stream credit, firing a timer, reading stats). Every other re-entry is refused with `E_REENTRANT` instead of deadlocking, in every build.

The synchronous call path is allocation-free once warm. A per-thread reply slot lets a synchronous method encode its whole reply into one reusable buffer, which is what moves a call through the C ABI to 49.8 ns ([ADR-028](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-028-synchronous-reply-slot.md)); a counting allocator in the tests holds the lending entry to zero allocations and a C ABI call to exactly one, the buffer it hands back.

## Threading

- **One mutator.** The core has one lock. Whoever holds it *is* the core loop. A synchronous call from the host runs on the caller's thread holding that lock, so it costs a mutex acquire, not a thread hop.
- **Async work.** Async calls are tasks on a small executor with no tokio, polled by the core thread, one task per in-flight call. Cancelling a call drops its future.
- **A blocking pool** runs blocking work off the lock. It must not write signals, and debug builds refuse such writes.
- **wasm is single threaded.** The host calls `keel_poll()` on the next microtask whenever the core asks to be scheduled.
- **Shutdown is orderly.** Every call still in flight is answered as cancelled and every stream ends, each exactly once, before the threads are joined.

## Transports and modes

| Mode | Where the core runs | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| in-process | linked into the app (C ABI on iOS, JNI on Android) | shipping |
| `wasm-main` | a wasm module on the page's main thread | simple web apps |
| `wasm-worker` | the same module in a worker | web apps that want the main thread free |
| `remote` | your machine, behind a WebSocket | `keel dev` |

Platform runtimes do the same jobs everywhere: load the core, allocate call ids, map replies to continuations, hold the mirror and apply change-sets on the main thread, implement observe and release, provide default adapters, implement the codecs, and **refuse a mismatched core** with a clear error that names both hashes.

## Compatibility

A UI and a core that were not built from the same schema must not talk. The schema hash is checked when the runtime attaches and surfaces as a typed mismatch error, and `keel bindgen --check` catches stale bindings at build time. Breaking the wire is a major version and needs an ADR; evolving a schema across a hash mismatch is deliberately not in v1.

## Diagnostics

Every macro mistake is an error with a stable code and a fixed shape: what happened, why, how to fix it, and where to read more. This one is verbatim from the test suite:

text

```
error[keel::E0012]: `Vec<Box<dyn Any>>` cannot cross the boundary
  = note: trait objects have no wire representation
  = help: make `items` a concrete `#[keel::api]` type, or an enum listing the cases you need
  = docs: https://keel.dev/errors/E0012
```

The catalogue, by family:

| Codes | What they catch |
| --- | --- |
| E0001 to E0008 | unsupported types, generics, lifetimes, trait objects, misplaced `Result` or `Stream`, bad map keys, unsupported item shapes, unknown attributes |
| E0010 to E0013 | error enums without messages, a store and its impl block that disagree, trait objects in fields, a store that cannot be restored automatically |
| E0020 to E0022 | `&mut self` or `self` receivers, non-`Send` async futures |
| E0030 to E0033 | port methods with non-wire parameters, invalid port shapes, an error type that cannot represent an unavailable port |
| E0040 to E0042 | query and mutation keys, signatures and return types |
| E0050 to E0052 | bindgen: duplicate names, names that collide after case conversion, clashes with the standard library |
| E0060 to E0064 | look-alike built-in names, aliased types, runtime port failures, `Option<Option<T>>`, objects used as values |

The CLI has its own `C00NN` codes with the same shape.

## The constitution

Twelve rules, enforced in review, not aspirational. They are the reason the project reads the way it does.

| Rule | In short | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **R1** | The schema is the only truth. A public type or function exists only if the schema can describe it. | Three languages cannot drift from each other if all three are derived from one description. |
| **R2** | `unsafe` lives in `keel-ffi` only, plus one schema loader in the CLI. Every block has a `// SAFETY:` comment; every other crate forbids it. | The audit surface is one crate, and it is the one reviewed under ASan and Miri. |
| **R3** | Generated code must pass native review: a Swift, Kotlin or TypeScript engineer who has never seen Rust would write it that way. Golden files lock it. | Adoption depends on the output feeling native, not generated. |
| **R4** | Every feature lands whole: unit tests, contract scenarios, a benchmark if the boundary is touched, docs on every `pub` item. | No half-features and no untested boundary. |
| **R5** | Reads never cross the boundary; writes cross once per transaction. No generated getter calls into the core. | This is the performance model. Everything else serves it. |
| **R6** | Nothing escapes as a panic or an abort. Every boundary entry is guarded; every error is a typed value. | A bug in the core must never take the app down with an unwinding crash. |
| **R7** | Compatibility is checked at load (schema hash) and at build. Breaking the wire is a major version and an ADR. | Mismatched halves are refused loudly instead of misdecoding quietly. |
| **R8** | Macro errors teach: a code, what, why, fix, docs link. | The Rust-side learning curve is the adoption risk. |
| **R9** | Budgets are tests. Benchmarks live in `bench/` and regressions fail CI. | Performance claims are kept true by the build, not by memory. |
| **R10** | We ship on it first: `examples/playground` uses only public APIs. | If the reference app needs a private door, the public API is wrong. |
| **R11** | Boundary changes need an ADR before code. | The wire, the runtime model, the threading model and generated shapes are expensive to change later. |
| **R12** | The core is deterministic: no wall clock, randomness or threads outside the Clock, Rng and Timer ports and the runtime. | Deterministic cores are testable with fakes and replayable. |

The engineering standards behind them: Rust 2024 edition with MSRV 1.85, `clippy -D warnings`, no `anyhow` in library crates, no `println!` in library code (logs go through the `Log` port), and no dependency that does not build for wasm32, iOS and Android.

## Decisions on record

The big decisions are written down as ADRs before the code. The ones in the tree today:

| ADR | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| [018](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-018-query-handles-and-dispatch-layer.md) | Query handles and the dispatch layer |
| [019](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-019-signals-transactional-delivery.md) | Signals: transactional delivery |
| [020](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-020-signals-delivery-order-and-round-cap.md) | Signals: delivery order and the round cap |
| [021](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-021-signals-contained-misuse.md) | Signals: contained misuse |
| [022](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-022-handle-generations-and-the-snapshot-floor.md) | Handle generations and the snapshot floor |
| [023](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-023-runtime-delivery-reentry-restore-and-shutdown.md) | Runtime delivery, re-entry, restore and shutdown |
| [024](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-024-standard-library-not-generated.md) | The standard library is not generated |
| [025](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-025-ports-typed-outcomes-and-schema-identity.md) | Ports: typed outcomes and schema identity |
| [026](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-026-ffi-host-contract-lifetimes-and-ownership.md) | The FFI host contract: lifetimes and ownership |
| [027](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-027-keyed-list-ops-are-recorded-not-diffed.md) | Keyed list operations are recorded, not diffed |
| [028](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/.10x/adrs/ADR-028-synchronous-reply-slot.md) | The synchronous reply slot |

## What v1 leaves out

By design, v1 has no sync engine, no hosted services and no shared UI of any kind. Kv is a foreign port rather than Rust-owned SQLite. Lazy lists are reserved and rejected. Those are choices recorded in the specification, not gaps.

## Read the source of truth

- [`docs/SPEC.md`](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/docs/SPEC.md): the binding specification for the wire, the ABI, the schema, the runtime model and the generated shapes. Code that disagrees with it is wrong.
- [`bench/RESULTS.md`](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/bench/RESULTS.md): every benchmark row, the machine, and what is still waiting for devices.
- [`.10x/reviews/`](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/tree/main/.10x/reviews): the four adversarial reviews of signals, runtime, macros and ffi.
- [`contract-tests/scenarios.md`](https://github.com/shreypdev/keel/blob/main/contract-tests/scenarios.md): the seventeen scenarios that define "the platforms agree".

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/api-swift.html

# API overview, Swift

Generated Swift is written the way a Swift engineer would write it by hand: value types, typed throws, async/await, AsyncSequence and an @Observable store. Swift 6 language mode, strict concurrency, no Objective-C.

`keel bindgen` writes a Swift package (`Sources/<Module>/Generated/*.swift` and a `Package.swift`) that depends only on `KeelRuntime`. The shapes below come from the playground's generated code and the specification (§10.1).

## Loading the core

Attach the app to its core once, before any store is created. The runtime checks the core's schema hash against the one the bindings were generated from and throws a clear error if they differ.

KeelBootstrap.swift

```swift
import KeelRuntime
import PlaygroundCore

@MainActor
static func start() throws {
    let adapters = Adapters.platformDefault              // URLSession, Keychain, files, …
        .replacing(PlaygroundNetwork.shared)             // swap one port
    try KeelCore.load(.inproc(adapters: adapters, expectedSchemaHash: KeelIds.schemaHash))
}
```

In debug builds you can attach to the core that `keel dev` serves instead, with `KeelCore.load(.remote(url: url, adapters: adapters, expectedSchemaHash: KeelIds.schemaHash))`. After loading, every generated type defaults to the shared core: `try Todos()` is `try Todos(ctx: .shared)`.

## Type mapping

| Rust | Swift |
| --- | --- |
| `bool`, `f32`, `f64` | `Bool`, `Float`, `Double` |
| `i8` … `i64`, `u8` … `u64` | `Int8` … `Int64`, `UInt8` … `UInt64` |
| `String`, `Bytes` | `String`, `[UInt8]` |
| `Duration`, `Timestamp`, `Uuid` | `Duration`, `Date`, `UUID` |
| `Option<T>`, `Vec<T>` | `T?`, `[T]` |
| `Map<K, V>` | `[K: V]` |
| record, enum, error | `struct`, `enum`, `enum` conforming to `Error` |

Names follow the platform: Rust `snake_case` becomes `camelCase` for methods and fields and `PascalCase` for types, and enum variants become `lowerCamel` cases.

## Records

A record is a `struct`: `Sendable`, `Hashable` and `Codable`, with a memberwise initializer.

swift

```swift
/// One item of the to-do list.
public struct Todo: KeelRecord, Sendable, Hashable, Codable {
    public var id: UUID
    public var title: String
    public var done: Bool

    public init(id: UUID, title: String, done: Bool)
}
```

The wire codec (`keelEncode`, `keelDecode`) is generated beside it and is not something you call.

## Enums

A unit enum is a `UInt16`-backed `enum` that is also `CaseIterable`, so it works directly in a `Picker`. A data enum carries its fields as associated values.

swift

```swift
public enum Filter: UInt16, KeelEnum, CaseIterable, Sendable, Codable {
    case all = 0, active = 1, done = 2
}

public enum Figure: KeelEnum, Sendable, Hashable {
    case circle(radius: Double)
    case rect(width: Double, height: Double)
    case label(String)
    case empty
}
```

## Errors

A Rust `#[keel::error]` becomes a Swift `enum` conforming to `Error` (and `LocalizedError`, with the message from `#[error("…")]`). Functions that can fail use **typed throws**.

swift

```swift
public enum TodoError: KeelError, Error, Sendable, Hashable {
    case emptyTitle            // "the title cannot be empty"
    // a variant that wraps another error carries it: case http(HttpError)
}

do {
    let todo = try await todos.add(title: draft)
} catch {
    // `error` is a TodoError, not a string to parse
    print(error.localizedDescription)
}
```

Typed throws needs Swift 6. `keel.toml` has `swift_typed_throws = false` for code that must still emit plain `throws`. A failure the shape of the API cannot express (a core panic, a malformed reply, schema drift) stops the process with a message, because it means the core and the bindings disagree.

## Objects and functions

An object is a `final class` holding a handle into the core. Sync methods are plain functions, async methods are `async`, and stream methods return an `AsyncThrowingStream`. A free Rust function is a free Swift function that takes the core last.

swift

```swift
public final class Probe: KeelObject, @unchecked Sendable {
    public init(ctx: KeelCore = .shared) throws            // the constructor `new`
    public func counters() -> ProbeCounters                // sync
    public func wait(ms: UInt32) async throws -> UInt32    // async
    public func ticks(count: UInt32) -> AsyncThrowingStream<UInt32, Error>   // stream
}

public func add(a: Int32, b: Int32, ctx: KeelCore = .shared) -> Int32
public func area(_ figure: Figure, ctx: KeelCore = .shared) throws(LabError) -> Double
```

Sync methods on an in-process core call straight into the core (`keel_call_sync`). Streams apply real backpressure: the generated code grants credit as your loop consumes items, and dropping the stream stops it in the core.

Release an object with `close()`, which is idempotent. `deinit` is only a backstop for objects that go out of scope without it, so hold an object for as long as you need its state.

## Stores

A store is an `@Observable` class on the `MainActor`. Every signal is a `public private(set) var`, so SwiftUI tracks reads and re-renders when a change-set is applied. Computed signals are read-only properties the core keeps up to date.

swift

```swift
@MainActor @Observable
public final class Todos: KeelStore {
    public private(set) var todos: [Todo]
    public private(set) var filter: Filter
    public private(set) var visible: [Todo]        // computed by the core
    public private(set) var remaining: UInt32      // computed by the core

    public init(ctx: KeelCore = .shared) throws
    public func setFilter(_ f: Filter)
    public func add(title: String) async throws(TodoError) -> Todo
}
```

Reading `todos.visible` is a plain property read: it never calls into the core. The initial values are decoded from the change-set the core emits when the store starts observing during `init`.

swift

```swift
struct TodosScreen: View {
    let todos: Todos
    var body: some View {
        List(todos.visible, id: \.id) { todo in
            Button(todo.title) { todos.toggle(id: todo.id) }
        }
        .toolbar { ToolbarItem(placement: .principal) { Text("\(todos.remaining) left") } }
    }
}
```

## Query handles

A `#[keel::query]` becomes a store with five signals: `data`, `status`, `error`, `fetching` and `updatedAt`, plus `refetch()` and `invalidate()`. Construct one to observe the query; it fetches when the data is missing or stale.

swift

```swift
let inbox = try RemoteTodosQueryHandle(list: "inbox")
// inbox.data: [RemoteTodo]?, inbox.status, inbox.fetching, inbox.error, inbox.updatedAt
```

See [Queries & mutations](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/queries.html) for what the core does behind it.

## Ports

The ten standard ports are implemented by `KeelRuntime` (`URLSession`, Keychain, `FileManager`, `NWPathMonitor` and so on) and are not generated into your module. A port you define yourself becomes a protocol your app implements and registers with the adapters:

swift

```swift
public protocol Http: KeelPort {
    func request(_ req: HttpRequest) async throws(HttpError) -> HttpResponse
}
```

See [Ports & adapters](https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/ports.html) for the defaults and for swapping one.

## Threading and lifetime

- Change-sets are applied on the `MainActor`, with per-frame coalescing, so observable properties only ever change on the main thread.
- Stores and objects release their handle on `close()`, with `deinit` as the backstop. `KeelCore.stats()` exposes live handle counts for tests.
- Swift 6 strict concurrency is on. Generated stores are `@MainActor`; objects are `@unchecked Sendable` because the core serializes access behind its lock.

---

Source: https://shreypdev.github.io/keel/docs/api-kotlin.html

# API overview, Kotlin

Generated Kotlin is what a Kotlin engineer would write by hand: data classes, sealed hierarchies, suspend functions, Flow, and StateFlows you read with collectAsState(). The runtime needs only the standard library and kotlinx-coroutines.

`keel bindgen` writes a Gradle module (`src/main/kotlin/<package>/*.kt`, a `build.gradle.kts` and a `.gitignore`) that depends only on `keel-runtime`. The shapes below come from the playground's generated code and the specification (§10.2).

## Loading the core

Attach the app to its core once per process, before any store is created, typically in `Application.onCreate`. `KeelCore.load` checks that the native library was built from the same schema as the bindings.

KeelApp.kt

```kotlin
class KeelApp : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        KeelCore.load(
            LoadOptions(
                expectedSchemaHash = KeelIds.SCHEMA_HASH,
                adapters = mapOf(StandardPorts.Http.PORT_ID to myHttp.portImpl()),
            ),
        )
    }
}
```

The core is `libkeel_core.so`, which `keel build --platform android` writes to `build/android/jniLibs/<abi>/`. On Android the runtime installs the adapters that need nothing from the platform (Clock, Rng, Log, Timer); pass the others you want to replace. After loading, every generated type defaults to the shared core: `Todos()` is `Todos(ctx = KeelCore.shared)`.

## Type mapping

| Rust | Kotlin |
| --- | --- |
| `bool`, `f32`, `f64` | `Boolean`, `Float`, `Double` |
| `i8` … `i64` | `Byte`, `Short`, `Int`, `Long` |
| `u8` … `u64` | `UByte`, `UShort`, `UInt`, `ULong` |
| `String`, `Bytes` | `String`, `ByteArray` |
| `Duration`, `Timestamp`, `Uuid` | `Duration`, `Timestamp`, `UUID` |
| `Option<T>`, `Vec<T>` | `T?`, `List<T>` |
| `Map<K, V>` | `Map<K, V>` |
| record, enum, error | `data class`, `enum class` or `sealed interface`, `sealed class` |

Names follow the platform: Rust `snake_case` becomes `camelCase` for functions and properties and `PascalCase` for types. Unit enum variants become `UPPER_SNAKE` constants; data enum variants become `PascalCase` classes. Keel does not support `Option<Option<T>>` because Kotlin cannot express nested optionality (`E0063`).

## Records

kotlin

```kotlin
/** One item of the to-do list. */
data class Todo(
    val id: UUID,
    val title: String,
    val done: Boolean,
) : KeelRecord
```

## Enums

A unit enum is an `enum class` with its wire index. A data enum is a `sealed interface` whose variants are data classes, `data object`s for the ones without fields.

kotlin

```kotlin
enum class Filter(val index: UShort) : KeelEnum {
    ALL(0u), ACTIVE(1u), DONE(2u);
}

sealed interface Figure : KeelEnum {
    data class Circle(val radius: Double) : Figure
    data class Rect(val width: Double, val height: Double) : Figure
    data class Label(val value: String) : Figure
    data object Empty : Figure
}
```

`when (figure)` over a sealed interface is exhaustive, so adding a variant in Rust is a compile error in every `when` that forgot it.

## Errors

A `#[keel::error]` becomes a `sealed class` extending `KeelException`, with the message from `#[error("…")]`. A failing `suspend` function throws the typed error, so `catch (e: TodoError)` and `when (e)` work.

kotlin

```kotlin
sealed class TodoError(message: String) : KeelException(message) {
    data object EmptyTitle : TodoError("the title cannot be empty")
    // a variant wrapping another error carries it: data class Http(val cause: HttpError)
}

viewModelScope.launch {
    try {
        store.add(draft)
    } catch (e: TodoError) {
        problem = when (e) {
            TodoError.EmptyTitle -> "Give it a title first."
        }
    }
}
```

## Objects and functions

An object is a class holding a handle into the core. Sync methods are plain functions, async methods are `suspend`, and stream methods return a `Flow`. A free Rust function is a top-level Kotlin function that takes the core as its last, defaulted parameter.

kotlin

```kotlin
class Probe private constructor(core: KeelCore, handle: Long) : KeelObject(core, handle) {
    fun counters(): ProbeCounters                       // sync
    suspend fun wait(ms: UInt): UInt                    // async, cancellable
    fun ticks(count: UInt): Flow<UInt>                  // stream
    companion object { fun create(ctx: KeelCore = KeelCore.shared): Probe }
}

fun add(a: Int, b: Int, ctx: KeelCore = KeelCore.shared): Int
suspend fun createRemoteTodo(list: String, title: String, ctx: KeelCore = KeelCore.shared): RemoteTodo
```
